prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
The national curriculum for England, revised in 2014, asks primary schools to teach joined handwriting. By Year 2, when children are six and seven, pupils are expected to start using the diagonal and horizontal strokes that join some letters. By the end of Year 6 they are expected to keep their writing legible in joined form when they write at speed. Other countries have gone the other way. The Common Core standards published in the United States in 2010 left cursive out, and many states followed. Since then several have restored it by law, California among them in 2023. Whether schools should keep teaching joined-up writing is therefore a live question and not a settled one. My view is that they should. The case for it does not depend on nostalgia. It depends on what a child needs from handwriting in the years when most school writing is still done by hand.

Those years are longer than people tend to assume. GCSE and A level examinations in England are written on paper, and so are most university exams in Britain. Ofqual has looked at on-screen exams, but handwritten papers remain the norm. A child who started Year 1 this September will sit GCSEs in 2037. In an exam hall that pupil has to produce several hundred words in an hour, and the examiner has to be able to read them. A slow or hard-to-read hand costs marks that the pupil's ideas have earned, and an examiner cannot give credit for a sentence that cannot be made out.

Joined writing is faster for a plain reason, which is that the pen leaves the paper less often. A child who prints lifts the pen at the end of every letter, and a child who joins lifts it at the end of every word. Adults who print can be quick, and I do not claim that joining is the only route to speed. Studies of pupils' writing in the United States found that many of them use a mixture of joined and printed letters. That is a good outcome. In my view it is more likely to come from having been taught the joins and then dropping the ones that slow the hand than from never having met them. Schools have a settled method for teaching joins, and a child who is taught it has a pattern to start from.

The stronger argument concerns fluency. Virginia Berninger and Steve Graham have studied children's handwriting in the United States for several decades. Their work has found that when handwriting is automatic, children write longer and better texts. The explanation is about attention. A child who has to think about how to form each letter has less attention left for choosing words, spelling them and ordering sentences. Handwriting becomes automatic only through practice, and practice needs a method to follow. A 2016 meta-analysis by Tanya Santangelo and Steve Graham found that teaching handwriting improved the legibility and fluency of pupils' writing. A school that gives no instruction leaves each child to invent a way of forming letters, and some of those ways are slow and hard to read.

The usual reply is that children will type for most of their adult lives, so time spent on pens is time wasted. I accept the premise and reject the conclusion. Typing should be taught, and my view is that it is taught better from about the age of nine or ten, when hands are large enough to reach a keyboard comfortably and when children can already spell and compose with some ease. Handwriting does not compete with it for much time. Practice takes a short slot, ten to fifteen minutes in many timetables, and the cost to the rest of the day is small.

There is also research suggesting that writing by hand does something typing does not. In a French study published in 2005, led by Marieke Longcamp, young children who learned letters by writing them recognised them better afterwards than children who learned them by typing. In 2014 Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer reported that students who took notes by hand answered conceptual questions better than students who typed, though later attempts to repeat the result have found smaller effects. In 2024 a team led by Audrey van der Meer in Norway recorded brain activity in 36 university students and found more widespread connectivity when they wrote by hand than when they typed. None of these studies is large, and none of them tests joined writing in particular. They support teaching handwriting. They do not on their own support teaching joins.

The case for joins therefore rests on narrower grounds. The first is the speed that comes from fewer pen lifts, described above. The second is spelling. Some teachers hold that writing a common ending such as -ing or -tion in one movement helps the hand and the memory to treat it as a unit. This is plausible, and I know of no firm evidence for it, so I offer it as something worth testing and not as a reason to decide the matter. The third is letter reversal. In most joined schemes every letter starts on the baseline with a small entry stroke, and some teachers report that this cuts down on b and d being swapped. That too is classroom experience and not a research finding.

Some children find joining hard. Children with dyspraxia or other motor difficulties may form letters slowly and tire quickly, and for them a keyboard or a simpler script can be the better tool. That is an argument for flexibility, and the English curriculum already allows for it. The Year 2 requirement is that children start to join some letters, which is a lower bar than joining all of them. A school that teaches joins to the class, accepts a legible print from a pupil who cannot manage them, and provides a keyboard where the difficulty is large is doing what I am arguing for. That is a different thing from removing joined writing from the curriculum for everyone.

A smaller point concerns reading. Teachers write on boards and in margins in a joined hand, and many parents and grandparents write that way in birthday cards. A child who has never been taught joins can still learn to read them, but it takes extra effort. Handwritten archives, from census returns to wartime letters, are mostly in joined script, and pupils who cannot read them depend on someone else's transcription. I would not rest the case on this, but it is a real cost of dropping the skill.

I would also set limits on what schools ask of children. Joining should begin once letters are formed reliably, which in England means Year 1 or Year 2. Lessons should be short and regular. The aim should be a legible, quick hand and not a perfect copperplate, and teachers who mark mainly for content, with legibility as a threshold, avoid turning neatness into a measure of ability. Keyboard skills should be taught alongside from about the age of nine. The evidence should also be watched. American states now differ in whether they require cursive, which gives researchers a natural comparison, and I would want to read the results of any study that used it.

Teaching joined handwriting costs little time and gives most children a faster, more automatic hand for the years when they write by hand. The evidence that handwriting matters is stronger than the evidence that joining matters, and I have said so. But the cost is low, and the arguments from exams and from fluency are concrete. On that balance primary schools should keep teaching it.
